analysis.one_liner: Blocks the SEC from requiring companies to disclose climate-related financial risks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The SEC had proposed a rule requiring publicly traded companies to tell investors about climate-related risks to their business. This bill would ban the agency from finalizing that rule, or any substantially similar one. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would benefit publicly traded corporations that would otherwise have to measure, audit, and disclose climate-related financial risks, with fossil fuel and other carbon-intensive firms having the most to hide from such disclosures. It would also spare them the compliance costs of the rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large public companies and carbon-intensive firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the SEC from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing its proposed climate disclosure rule, or any substantially similar rule, removing an upcoming compliance obligation for registrants.
The proposed rule the bill targets would require registrants to disclose their climate-related risks, so blocking it means companies never have to produce that information for investors.

analysis.who_pays: Investors, including ordinary people whose retirement savings are invested in public companies, who would continue buying securities without standardized information about how climate risks could affect those companies' value. The public also bears the cost of climate risks being priced less accurately in markets.

drawbacks.text: Climate disclosure rules impose real measuring, auditing, and reporting costs on companies, and disclosures about climate risk can expose firms to litigation, which is the strongest good-faith case for blocking the rule.

Opponents of SEC climate rules have also argued the agency was stretching its statutory authority into matters Congress did not authorize, a legal objection raised in broader litigation over the rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes almost entirely to regulated companies, in the form of avoided compliance costs and avoided scrutiny. The cost falls on investors who lose standardized climate-risk information. There is no compensating benefit for ordinary people in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The SEC proposed the climate disclosure rule on April 11, 2022, requiring registrants to disclose their climate-related risks.
Rep. French Hill introduced H.R. 8589 on July 29, 2022, to prohibit the SEC from finalizing that rule or any substantially similar rule.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on July 29, 2022, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies that would have faced the SEC's climate disclosure requirements were better off with the bill dead in committee, since the agency remained free to proceed with its rulemaking.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that would have faced disclosure rules

for.name: Rep. French Hill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block the SEC's climate disclosure rule.

against.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
against.what_they_did: Proposed the climate disclosure rule the bill sought to block, keeping the rulemaking alive while the bill sat in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have spared these companies the cost of measuring and disclosing climate-related financial risks. Their gain comes directly out of investors' access to that information, including ordinary people's retirement savings.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and other carbon-intensive firms
industries.note: These firms have the most climate risk to disclose and would have benefited most from a ban on the rule. Blocking disclosure lets climate-related threats to company value stay out of view.

The proposed rule was written for investors, who would lose standardized climate-risk data if the bill had passed. Asset managers that rely on this data for risk models would also have lost a standardized input.
